paras: The Brightwood Y.M.C.A. mob threat was an episode on the night of Saturday, 17 October 1903, in which an unnamed Black man was stabbed in a fight at the Brightwood Railroad Y.M.C.A. building in Indiana and then pursued by a mob that threatened to lynch him. He escaped on a street car and was not seen again, and the episode is known from a single short item in the Indianapolis Journal.

According to the Indianapolis Journal, the man entered the Y.M.C.A. building and asked for alms, was refused, and "became abusive." A fight followed, which the paper said he started, and in it he was stabbed several times; the item does not say who stabbed him. He ran from the building and took refuge in a grocery store run by Louis Grim, where he was followed by "a howling mob" and threatened with lynching. "After much difficulty," in the paper's words, he boarded a street car and got away.

By the following Tuesday his name had not been learned, although the Journal said efforts had been made to locate him. A rumor that he was a railroad detective in disguise circulated, but railroad authorities discredited it and said they believed he was "a colored tramp." No report of arrests of anyone in the mob, or of any official inquiry into the stabbing, appears in the coverage.

The Indianapolis Journal ran the story on page 6 on 20 October 1903 under the headline "Black Beggar Abusive." The item placed the blame for the fight on the man, calling him "the negro" and repeating the railroad's description of him as a tramp, while it reported the mob and the lynching threat without comment. No other white paper and no Black paper was found to have carried the episode.

bases: A1 reports a 'howling mob' pursued a stabbed Black man and that he 'was threatened with lynching'; he escaped, so the episode is a threatened lynching, not a completed one.
A1 reports that the man escaped on a street car and was not seen again, so no one was killed; the mob's threat had no lawful authority, but no killing occurred.
Only one Indianapolis Journal item (A1), published three days later, reports the episode; no other white or Black paper was found.
